Q7. What organs can pre-eclampsia affect?

blocks.text: **Brain, liver, kidney, blood, lungs and placenta.**

content_groups.group_title: Q8. What blood tests would you request?

blocks.text: “FBC with platelets, renal function and liver function tests, with additional tests such as haemolysis markers where HELLP is suspected.”

content_groups.group_title: Q9. What fetal complications can occur?

blocks.text: “Fetal growth restriction, oligohydramnios, placental abruption, fetal compromise and stillbirth.”

content_groups.group_title: Q10. What is the definitive treatment for pre-eclampsia?

blocks.text: **Delivery of the placenta**, i.e. delivery of the pregnancy.
Timing depends on gestational age, maternal condition and fetal condition.

content_groups.group_title: Q11. What is the definitive treatment for hypertension itself?

blocks.text: Antihypertensives control BP but do not cure pre-eclampsia.
**Delivery is the definitive treatment for pre-eclampsia, but stabilisation and management are required before delivery.**

**“I would first confirm the blood pressure using appropriate technique and establish when the hypertension was diagnosed. If it occurred before 20 weeks, I would consider chronic hypertension. If it developed after 20 weeks, I would assess for proteinuria and maternal or uteroplacental organ dysfunction to distinguish gestational hypertension from pre-eclampsia. I would ask specifically about headache, visual symptoms, epigastric or right upper quadrant pain and shortness of breath. Investigations would include FBC and platelets, renal and liver function and appropriate assessment of proteinuria, together with fetal growth and wellbeing assessment. Severe hypertension requires urgent antihypertensive treatment. I would manage the mother and fetus together and involve the senior obstetric team when there are severe features or fetal compromise.”**
Control BP + assess mother/fetus + determine timing of delivery.

**“The key distinction is not simply whether a pregnant woman has hypertension, but whether the hypertension is chronic, gestational, or associated with maternal or uteroplacental dysfunction consistent with pre-eclampsia.”**
